reasoning: Long oo: jooz, a collective noun for walnuts. The same spelling can also mean husband, but the English fixes the meaning as walnuts.

The sulha is the well-known Palestinian custom of tribal reconciliation. ص is emphatic (S) and the vowel is u. Taa marbuta after ح is written e by the scheme's rule, though some speakers end it closer to a.
The country name is ba7reen (normally il-ba7reen with the article). The -ayn ending becomes -een in Palestinian speech.
Common Palestinian thanks to someone who is working, literally 'may God give you health'. Urban speakers say yi3Tiik with yi-. m3allim (boss, master craftsman) may also be heard as mi3allim.
The transitive verb rajja3 (give back) takes the feminine ending -ti plus li 'to me', giving rajja3tili (masculine would be rajja3tilli). ط is a sun letter, so iT-Tanjara.

meaning_fix: skirt (from French jupe); the usual word for pocket is جيب jeeb
reasoning: In Levantine speech jeebe mostly means a skirt, while pocket is jeeb. I am less sure how far jeebe is also used for pocket in Ramallah.
Everyday Palestinian 3ashaan, for both 'because' and 'in order to'. Long second aa.
The correlative 'laa X wala Y' is used in colloquial Palestinian, and wala is also common on its own. The ellipsis is not romanized.
ma7bas is the plumbing shut-off valve, as in ma7bas il-mayy. The same word can also mean a ring, but the English fixes the sense as valve.
Standard Palestinian word for mosquito, with the collective naamuus. Taa marbuta after س is written e.
Short i, then br. Taa marbuta after ر is a.
Construct state, so the taa marbuta is pronounced t: kurat 'adam. ق in قدم is a glottal stop in this everyday word. With the article it is kurat il-'adam.

meaning_fix: There is no might or power except through God (said in dismay, exasperation or resignation)
palestinian_alternative: لا حول ولا قوة إلا بالله
reasoning: The entry looks like a truncation of the fixed formula laa 7awla wala 'uwwe illa billaah. It expresses dismay or resignation rather than literally 'Oh my God'. The romanization follows the spelling as given.

Widely used Levantine proverb. The colloquial plural is Tyuur, ط is a sun letter, and the imperfect of waqa3 is ti'a3 with a glottal ق. The exact colloquial vowels of this semi-fixed proverb are less certain.
heek 'like this' is the Palestinian form (not hekke or hayda). Common phrase meaning 'that's why'.
Form II verb 'he cleaned'. Palestinian pronounces ظ in this word as an emphatic D and doubles it, so naDDaf (as in naDiif 'clean'). The vowelling is respelled with ض to match.
Typical Palestinian and Jordanian word for man or guy, plural zalam. Taa marbuta after م is e.
Blessing said when something good, such as a wedding or engagement, is in progress. yitammimlak is the Form II verb plus 'for you (m.)'. خير is kheer in Palestinian.
An MSA-origin economic and technical term that Palestinians do use in conversation, as in istihlaak il-kahraba. The initial hamza is only a vowel seat, so it is written as i.
ق is a glottal stop and ن is doubled. The first vowel varies ('inniine or 'anniine), and I am not fully certain of the Ramallah vowel. zujaaje and shiishe are other words for bottle.
il- stays il- before ف. Taa marbuta after ح is written e by the scheme's rule. Palestinians say 'read the faati7a' for the ritual recitation at a death or grave.
Active participle 'late', with a medial hamza written ' and a doubled kh. Spelling follows the scheme's own example.
Pattern fa3uul from 7i'id 'grudge'. ق is a glottal stop in this everyday word and the last vowel is long uu. It also means grudge-bearing or resentful.
khalli + ni gives khalliini, with a doubled l and a long ii. at'akkad is the 1st-person subjunctive with a glottal stop. Many speakers drop that glottal stop.
Palestinian 7awaaleen, used for spatial 'around' as in 7awaaleen il-beet. Lebanese uses 7awaali.
